title: Matrix5.02
notes: $$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ bc & ca & ab \end{vmatrix} = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ bc & ca & ab \end{vmatrix}$$
Applying column operations $C_1 \to C_1 - C_2$ and $C_2 \to C_2 - C_3$:
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ a-b & b-c & c \\ bc-ca & ca-ab & ab \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \\ b+c & c+a & a+b \end{vmatrix} = (b-c)(c-a)(a-b)(a+b+c)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \\ b+c & c+a & a+b \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \\ a+b+c & a+b+c & a+b+c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (a+b+c) \begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (a+b+c) \begin{vmatrix} a-b & b-c & c \\ a^2-b^2 & b^2-c^2 & c^2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ a^3 & b^3 & c^3 \end{vmatrix} = (b-c)(c-a)(a-b)(a+b+c)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ a^3 & b^3 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ a-b & b-c & c \\ a^3-b^3 & b^3-c^3 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
Factoring $x^3 - y^3 = (x-y)(x^2 + xy + y^2)$, take $(a-b)$ common from $C_1$ and $(b-c)$ common from $C_2$:
$$\begin{vmatrix} x & y & z \\ x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ yz & zx & xy \end{vmatrix} = (y-z)(z-x)(x-y)(yz+zx+xy)$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} x & y & z \\ x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ yz & zx & xy \end{vmatrix}$$
Multiply $R_1, R_2, R_3$ by $x, y, z$ respectively and divide by $xyz$:
$$= \frac{1}{xyz} \begin{vmatrix} x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ x^3 & y^3 & z^3 \\ xyz & xyz & xyz \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \frac{xyz}{xyz} \begin{vmatrix} x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ x^3 & y^3 & z^3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ x^3 & y^3 & z^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ x^2-y^2 & y^2-z^2 & z^2 \\ x^3-y^3 & y^3-z^3 & z^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (x-y)(y-z) \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ x+y & y+z & z^2 \\ x^2+xy+y^2 & y^2+yz+z^2 & z^3 \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\begin{vmatrix} b+c & a & b \\ c+a & c & a \\ a+b & b & c \end{vmatrix} = (a+b+c)(a-c)^2$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} b+c & a & b \\ c+a & c & a \\ a+b & b & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} (b+c)-a-b & a & b \\ (c+a)-c-a & c & a \\ (a+b)-b-c & b & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix} c-a & a & b \\ 0 & c & a \\ -(c-a) & b & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (c-a) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & b \\ 0 & c & a \\ -1 & b & c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (c-a) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & b \\ 0 & c & a \\ 0 & a+b & b+c \end{vmatrix}$$
$$\text{LHS} = \begin{vmatrix} 1+a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ a_1 & 1+a_2 & a_3 \\ a_1 & a_2 & 1+a_3 \end{vmatrix}$$
Key Determinant Properties Used in These Proofs
Property 1: Adding a multiple of one row/column to another does not change the determinant value.
Property 2: Taking a common factor from any row or column: $$\begin{vmatrix} ka & kb \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = k\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix}$$
Property 3: If a row/column is a sum of two terms, the determinant splits into two determinants.
Property 4: Interchanging two rows/columns changes the sign of the determinant.
Strategy tip: In every proof above, the key move is to create zeros by column/row operations (C1 → C1 − C2, etc.), then factor common terms and expand along the row/column with the most zeros.
confusion: When factoring a common term from a row or column, it is divided OUT of the determinant, not multiplied. Forgetting this leads to off-by-a-factor errors.

Column operations C1 → C1 − C2 change the determinant structure but preserve its value. However, C1 → C1 + C2 ALSO preserves value — both are valid since the operation adds a multiple of one column to another.

When two rows become proportional after operations, the determinant is zero — this is a useful check. Do not confuse proportional rows with identical rows (both give zero, but proportional is a more general condition).
The Vandermonde determinant result (1, x, x^2 pattern) = (y−z)(z−x)(x−y) is a frequently tested identity — memorize its pattern.
practice: Prove that |[1,1,1],[a,b,c],[a^2,b^2,c^2]| = (b−a)(c−a)(c−b). Hint: use column operations.
If a+b+c = 0, prove that |[a,b,c],[c,a,b],[b,c,a]| = a^3 + b^3 + c^3 − 3abc = 3abc (since a+b+c=0 implies a^3+b^3+c^3 = 3abc).
Evaluate |[1+a, b, c],[a, 1+b, c],[a, b, 1+c]| using the property C1 → C1 + C2 + C3.
universalFacts: Determinant proofs at this level always use the same 3-4 properties in combination. Master them and you can solve any proof.
The most common strategy is: create zeros via row/column operations, factor common terms, then expand along the row/column with the most zeros.
If a+b+c = 0, then a^3+b^3+c^3 = 3abc. This algebraic identity frequently appears as a step in determinant proofs.
The Vandermonde determinant |[1,1,1],[a,b,c],[a^2,b^2,c^2]| = (a−b)(a−c)(b−c) is one of the most important determinant identities in competitive mathematics.
